cards.name: Copulative Conjunction
cards.eli5: The “and” word. It just adds the next thing on.
cards.oneLine: Joins two equal elements by adding one to the other.
cards.mnemonic: And · Or · But · So · For — And: copulative.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Copulative, as in couple — it couples two carriages together. Plain addition, no contrast, no reason.
cards.spotIt: Can you read it as plain “and”, with nothing contrasting and nothing following from what went before?
cards.bookDef: καί (“and,” “also”); δέ (“and”); οὐδέ (“and not”); μηδέ (“and not”); τέ (“and so”); οὔτε (“and not”); μήτε (“and not”).
cards.watchOut: τε is overwhelmingly a word of Acts, and τε … τε (or τε … καί) can mean “not only … but also”: ἐθνῶν τε καὶ βασιλέων υἱῶν τε Ἰσραήλ, “to Gentiles, kings, and the Israelites” (Acts 9:15). And δέ is on two rows of the chart — “and” here, “but” under adversative. Context decides.

examples.greek: ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος, *καὶ* ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν, *καὶ* θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος
examples.english: In the beginning was the Word, *and* the Word was with God, *and* the Word was God
examples.note: Each καί adds a clause of equal weight. Nothing contrasts, nothing is inferred — three statements, coupled.

cards.name: Disjunctive Conjunction
cards.eli5: The “or” word. This one, or that one.
cards.oneLine: Joins two elements as alternatives.
cards.mnemonic: And · Or · But · So · For — Or: disjunctive.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Dis-junctive: it joins by setting apart. Railway points 🔀 — the train goes down one line or the other.
cards.spotIt: Would “or” (or “whether”) fit, offering a choice between the two?
cards.bookDef: ἤ (“or”); εἴτε (“if,” “whether”).
cards.watchOut: ἤ after a comparative is “than”, not “or”: μᾶλλον ἤ, “rather than”. That is comparison, not a choice.

examples.greek: Μὴ νομίσητε ὅτι ἦλθον καταλῦσαι τὸν νόμον *ἢ* τοὺς προφήτας
examples.english: Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law *or* the Prophets
examples.note: ἤ offers two alternatives — the Law, or the Prophets — and denies both.

cards.name: Adversative Conjunction
cards.eli5: The “but” word. It sets the next bit against the last.
cards.oneLine: Joins two elements in contrast.
cards.mnemonic: And · Or · But · So · For — But: adversative.
cards.mnemonicWhy: An adversary is the one set against you. The adversative sets one clause against the other: not this, but that.
cards.spotIt: Would “but”, “yet” or “except” fit — and does the second half push against the first?
cards.bookDef: ἀλλά (“but”); δέ (“but”); μέν (“but”); μέντοι (“nevertheless”); πλήν (“but,” “except”); εἰ μή (“except”); ὅμως (“yet”); καίτοι (“yet”).
cards.watchOut: δέ is the chameleon: “and” (copulative) or “but” (adversative), and often barely more than a pause. μέν on its own is rarely translated; it sets up a following δέ — “on the one hand … on the other”.

examples.greek: ἵνα πᾶς ὁ πιστεύων εἰς αὐτὸν μὴ ἀπόληται *ἀλλ᾽* ἔχῃ ζωὴν αἰώνιον
examples.english: that whoever believes in him should not perish *but* have eternal life
examples.note: ἀλλά after a negative: not perish, but have life. The strongest “but” in Greek.

cards.name: Inferential Conjunction
cards.eli5: The “so” word. Because of all that, here is what follows.
cards.oneLine: Draws a conclusion from what came before.
cards.mnemonic: And · Or · But · So · For — So: inferential.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Infer: to draw a conclusion. The signal ➡️ says the line goes on from here because of what came before.
cards.spotIt: Would “therefore” or “so” fit, and does the clause follow as a conclusion from the one before?
cards.bookDef: οὖν (“therefore,” “so”); ἄρα (“then”); διό (“for this reason”); δή (“therefore”).
cards.watchOut: οὖν in narrative, especially John, is often just “then” or “so” moving the story on, not a logical inference. Ask whether the clause really follows from the last one.

examples.english: I appeal to you *therefore*, brothers
examples.note: οὖν turns eleven chapters of doctrine into a conclusion: because of all that, therefore this.

cards.name: Explanatory Conjunction
cards.eli5: The “for” word. Here is why I just said that.
cards.oneLine: Introduces an explanation of, or ground for, what came before.
cards.mnemonic: And · Or · But · So · For — For: explanatory.
cards.mnemonicWhy: γάρ gives the explanation — the timetable 📋 that says why the train is running. It points backwards, the opposite way from οὖν.
cards.spotIt: Would “for” fit, with the clause explaining or grounding the one before it? γάρ is postpositive: it never stands first.
cards.bookDef: γάρ (“for”).
cards.watchOut: οὖν looks forward — “so, therefore”. γάρ looks back — “for, because of what I just said”. The two are opposite arrows.

examples.greek: Οὕτως *γὰρ* ἠγάπησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν κόσμον
examples.english: *For* God so loved the world
examples.note: γάρ explains 3:15: whoever believes has eternal life, because this is how God loved the world. Second word in the sentence, as always.

cards.name: Purpose Conjunction
cards.eli5: Why did you do it? “In order THAT …” The aim.
cards.oneLine: Introduces the intended aim of the main clause.
cards.mnemonic: In order that · So that · Because · As · If · Even if · That · When · Where — In order that: purpose.
cards.mnemonicWhy: A target 🎯 — the arrow has not landed yet. Purpose is what someone meant to happen. ἵνα is the purpose word, usually with a subjunctive.
cards.spotIt: Can you put “in order that” in front of it without changing the sense? Then it is the aim, not the outcome.
cards.bookDef: ἵνα (“in order that,” “so that”); ὅπως (“that”).

examples.greek: *ἵνα* πᾶς ὁ πιστεύων εἰς αὐτὸν μὴ ἀπόληται
examples.english: *in order that* whoever believes in him should not perish
examples.note: ἵνα gives what God meant by giving the Son: the aim was that believers not perish.

cards.name: Result Conjunction
cards.eli5: What came of it? “SO THAT …” The outcome.
cards.oneLine: Introduces the outcome of the main clause.
cards.mnemonic: In order that · So that · Because · As · If · Even if · That · When · Where — So that: result.
cards.mnemonicWhy: A bang 💥 — the arrow has landed. Result is what actually came of it, intended or not. ὥστε is the result word, often with an infinitive.
cards.spotIt: Would “with the result that” fit? Then it is the outcome, not the aim.
cards.bookDef: ὥστε (“so that”); ὅπως (“that”).
cards.watchOut: ὅπως is on the chart twice — purpose and result — and ἵνα can drift into result too. The word does not settle it; ask whether it was the aim or the outcome.

examples.greek: Οὕτως γὰρ ἠγάπησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν κόσμον, *ὥστε* τὸν υἱὸν τὸν μονογενῆ ἔδωκεν
examples.english: For God so loved the world, *that* he gave his only Son
examples.note: ὥστε gives what his love led to: the giving of the Son. And ὥστε with an indicative, ἔδωκεν, stresses that it actually happened.

cards.name: Causal Conjunction
cards.eli5: The “because” word. Here is the reason.

filled: blessed are the poor in spirit

cards.oneLine: Introduces the cause or reason for the main clause.
cards.mnemonic: In order that · So that · Because · As · If · Even if · That · When · Where — Because: causal.
cards.mnemonicWhy: A root 🌱 — the thing underneath that makes the rest grow. διότι is διὰ τοῦτο ὅτι squashed together: “because of this, that”.
cards.spotIt: Would “because” or “since” fit, giving the reason for the main clause?
cards.bookDef: ὅτι (“that,” “because”); διότι (“because”); ἐπεί (“because,” “since”); ἐπειδή (“because”).
cards.watchOut: ὅτι is on the chart twice: causal (“because”) and declarative (“that”). After a verb of saying, thinking, knowing or seeing it is almost always declarative.

examples.greek: Μακάριοι οἱ πτωχοὶ τῷ πνεύματι, *ὅτι* αὐτῶν ἐστιν ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν
examples.english: Blessed are the poor in spirit, *for* theirs is the kingdom of heaven
examples.note: ὅτι gives the reason they are blessed. English often says “for”, but it is cause, not γάρ-style explanation.

cards.name: Comparative Conjunction
cards.eli5: The “just as” word. This is like that.
cards.oneLine: Introduces a comparison: one thing is like another.
cards.mnemonic: In order that · So that · Because · As · If · Even if · That · When · Where — As: comparative.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Twins 👯 — one clause set beside another it matches. ὡς is “as”; add -περ for emphasis and you get ὥσπερ, “just as”; καθ-ώς is “according as”.
cards.spotIt: Would “as”, “like” or “just as” fit, laying one thing alongside another?
cards.bookDef: ὡς (“as,” “like”); ὥσπερ (“just as”); καθώς (“as,” “just as”); καθάπερ (“just as”).

examples.english: that you love one another *just as* I have loved you
examples.note: καθώς sets the pattern: their love is to match his.

cards.name: Conditional Conjunction
cards.eli5: The “if” word. This happens only if that happens.
cards.oneLine: Introduces the condition (protasis) of a conditional sentence.
cards.mnemonic: In order that · So that · Because · As · If · Even if · That · When · Where — If: conditional.
cards.mnemonicWhy: A traffic light 🚦 — go only if it is green. εἰ with the indicative, ἐάν with the subjunctive: the classes of condition start here.
cards.spotIt: Would “if” fit? Then check the mood: εἰ + indicative is first or second class, ἐάν + subjunctive third, εἰ + optative fourth.
cards.bookDef: εἰ (“if”); ἐάν (“if”); εἴπερ (“if indeed”).
cards.watchOut: εἰ καί and καὶ εἰ are concessive — “even if” — not plain conditions. And εἰ μή is “except”, filed under adversative.

examples.greek: *ἐὰν* ὁμολογῶμεν τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν, πιστός ἐστιν καὶ δίκαιος
examples.english: *If* we confess our sins, he is faithful and just
examples.note: ἐάν + the subjunctive ὁμολογῶμεν: a third class condition, a real “if”.

cards.name: Concessive Conjunction
cards.eli5: The “even though” word. It is true, and it still does not stop the rest.
cards.oneLine: Concedes a point that might have stopped the main clause, and says it did not.
cards.mnemonic: In order that · So that · Because · As · If · Even if · That · When · Where — Even if: concessive.
cards.mnemonicWhy: A shrug 🤷 — granted, and yet. καί + εἰ = “even if”; καίπερ is “although”, nearly always with a participle.
cards.spotIt: Would “although”, “even though” or “even if” fit? Look for καί glued to εἰ, or καίπερ.
cards.bookDef: εἰ καί (“even if”); καὶ εἰ (“even if”); κἄν (“even though”); καίπερ (“although”).

examples.greek: *καίπερ* ὢν υἱός, ἔμαθεν ἀφ᾽ ὧν ἔπαθεν τὴν ὑπακοήν
examples.english: *Although* he was a Son, he learned obedience through what he suffered
examples.note: καίπερ with the participle ὤν: being a Son might have exempted him, and it did not.

cards.name: Declarative Conjunction
cards.eli5: The “that” word after saying or thinking. It opens up what was said or thought.
cards.oneLine: Introduces the content of what is said, thought, known or seen.
cards.mnemonic: In order that · So that · Because · As · If · Even if · That · When · Where — That: declarative.
cards.mnemonicWhy: A speech bubble 💬 — the ὅτι opens it and the words inside are the content. Sometimes it is left untranslated and the bubble is just quotation marks.
cards.spotIt: Is there a verb of saying, thinking, knowing, seeing or hearing just before? Then ὅτι (or ἵνα) gives its content.
cards.bookDef: ὅτι (“that”); ἵνα (“that”). Conjunctions sometimes untranslated or communicated with a dash, colon, or quotation marks.

examples.greek: ἐάν τις εἴπῃ *ὅτι* Ἀγαπῶ τὸν θεόν
examples.english: If anyone says, *“*I love God”
examples.note: ὅτι after εἴπῃ opens the quotation and is not translated — English uses quotation marks. This is the chart’s own point.

cards.name: Temporal Conjunction
cards.eli5: The “when” word. It says when the main thing happened.
cards.oneLine: Introduces the time of the main clause.
cards.mnemonic: In order that · So that · Because · As · If · Even if · That · When · Where — When: temporal.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Tempus, time: the clock ⏰. ὅτε “when”, ὅταν “whenever” (ὅτε + ἄν, so the subjunctive follows), ἕως “until”, πρίν “before”.
cards.spotIt: Would “when”, “whenever”, “until” or “before” fit?
cards.bookDef: ὅτε (“when”); ἕως (“until”); ὅταν (“whenever”); πρίν (“before”).

examples.greek: *ὅτε* δὲ ἦλθεν τὸ πλήρωμα τοῦ χρόνου, ἐξαπέστειλεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ
examples.english: But *when* the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son
examples.note: ὅτε says when God sent: at the fullness of time.

cards.name: Local Conjunction
cards.eli5: The “where” word. It says where.
cards.oneLine: Introduces the place of the main clause.
cards.mnemonic: In order that · So that · Because · As · If · Even if · That · When · Where — Where: local.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Local, as in location — a pin 📍. The -ου ending is the old “where” ending: οὗ, ὅπου, ποῦ.
cards.spotIt: Would “where” or “from where” fit?
cards.bookDef: οὗ (“where”); ὅπου (“where”); ὅθεν (“from where,” “whence”).
cards.watchOut: ὅθεν can also be inferential — “therefore”, “for which reason”, as often in Hebrews. From where → from which.

examples.greek: *ὅπου* γάρ ἐστιν ὁ θησαυρός σου, ἐκεῖ ἔσται καὶ ἡ καρδία σου
examples.english: For *where* your treasure is, there your heart will be also
examples.note: ὅπου gives the place, and ἐκεῖ “there” picks it up in the main clause.

cards.name: Adverb Modifying a Verb
cards.eli5: It tells you more about the doing. “Divorce her SECRETLY.” Any kind of doing-word will take one.
cards.oneLine: The adverb modifies a verb — indicative, infinitive, participle, imperative or subjunctive alike.
cards.mnemonic: Verb · Adjective · Adverb — Verb: an adverb modifying a verb.
cards.mnemonicWhy: That is what the name says: ad-verb, added to the verb. The chart’s point is that the mood does not matter — every one of the five takes an adverb.
cards.spotIt: Find the verb or verbal (infinitive, participle) it sits next to. Does the adverb say when, how much, how or where it was done?
cards.bookDef: Adverbs modifying a verb: indicative, infinitive, participle, imperative, subjunctive.

examples.english: Death will be no *more* (NRSV)
examples.note: ἔτι modifies the indicative ἔσται.

examples.english: Joseph … decided to divorce her *secretly*
examples.note: λάθρᾳ modifies the infinitive ἀπολῦσαι, not ἐβουλήθη: he decided openly to divorce her quietly.

examples.english: The person who sows *sparingly* will also reap sparingly
examples.note: The first φειδομένως modifies the participle σπείρων; the second modifies the future indicative θερίσει.

examples.english: be ready *in season* and *out of season* (ESV)
examples.note: Two adverbs modifying the imperative ἐπίστηθι — when it suits and when it does not.

examples.greek: ἵνα … *σωφρόνως* καὶ *δικαίως* καὶ *εὐσεβῶς* ζήσωμεν ἐν τῷ νῦν αἰῶνι
examples.english: to live in a *sensible*, *righteous*, and *godly* way in the present age
examples.note: Three -ως adverbs modifying the subjunctive ζήσωμεν. -ως is the adverb ending, like English -ly.

cards.name: Adverb Modifying an Adjective
cards.eli5: It turns up a describing word. Not just violent — SO violent.
cards.oneLine: The adverb intensifies or qualifies an adjective.
cards.mnemonic: Verb · Adjective · Adverb — Adjective: an adverb modifying an adjective.
cards.mnemonicWhy: A volume knob on a describing word. λίαν, “very, exceedingly”, is the chart’s example twice over — here on an adjective, next on an adverb.
cards.spotIt: Is the adverb sitting next to an adjective and changing how much of it there is?
cards.bookDef: Adverbs modifying an adjective.
cards.watchOut: Not the same as an adverb used AS an adjective (τῷ νῦν καιρῷ). Here the adverb is modifying an adjective that is already there.

examples.greek: [ἦσαν] χαλεποὶ *λίαν*, ὥστε μὴ ἰσχύειν τινὰ παρελθεῖν διὰ τῆς ὁδοῦ ἐκείνης
examples.english: They were *so* violent that no one could pass that way
examples.note: λίαν modifies the adjective χαλεποί: not merely violent, exceedingly violent.

cards.name: Adverb Modifying an Adverb
cards.eli5: One adverb turning up another. Not just early — VERY early.
cards.oneLine: The adverb intensifies or qualifies another adverb.
cards.mnemonic: Verb · Adjective · Adverb — Adverb: an adverb modifying an adverb.
cards.mnemonicWhy: A knob on a knob. Mark 1:35 stacks three: πρωΐ “early”, ἔννυχα “at night”, and λίαν turning them up.
cards.spotIt: Is the adverb next to another adverb, and adjusting how much of it?
cards.bookDef: Adverbs modifying an adverb.

examples.greek: καὶ πρωῒ ἔννυχα *λίαν* ἀναστὰς ἐξῆλθεν καὶ ἀπῆλθεν εἰς ἔρημον τόπον
examples.english: *Very* early in the morning, while it was still dark, he got up, went out, and made his way to a deserted place
examples.note: λίαν modifies the adverbs πρωῒ ἔννυχα: not just early, very early.

cards.name: Adverb of Time
cards.eli5: It says WHEN. Afterward, now, then, still.
cards.oneLine: Answers the question “when?”.
cards.mnemonic: When · How much · How · Where — When: time.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The clock 🕰️. ἔπειτα “then, afterward”, νῦν “now”, ἔτι “still”, πάντοτε “always”, σήμερον “today”.
cards.spotIt: Ask “when?” of the verb. If the adverb is the answer, it is time.
cards.bookDef: Time (When?)

examples.greek: *ἔπειτα* ἦλθον εἰς τὰ κλίματα τῆς Συρίας καὶ τῆς Κιλικίας
examples.english: *Afterward*, I went to the regions of Syria and Cilicia
examples.note: ἔπειτα says when he went: after the Jerusalem visit of 1:18.

cards.name: Adverb of Degree
cards.eli5: It says HOW MUCH. Very, more, abundantly.
cards.oneLine: Answers the question “how much?” or “to what extent?”.
cards.mnemonic: When · How much · How · Where — How much: degree.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The volume knob 🔊. λίαν “very”, μᾶλλον “more”, περισσῶς “exceedingly”, σφόδρα “greatly”.
cards.spotIt: Ask “how much?” or “how far?”. If the adverb is the answer, it is degree.
cards.bookDef: Degree (How much?)
cards.watchOut: Degree and manner blur. “How much?” is degree; “in what way?” is manner. λίαν is always degree.

examples.greek: ἐγὼ ἦλθον ἵνα ζωὴν ἔχωσιν καὶ *περισσὸν* ἔχωσιν
examples.english: I came that they may have life, and have it *abundantly* (NASB)
examples.note: περισσόν, a neuter adjective doing an adverb’s job, says how much life: more than enough.

cards.name: Adverb of Manner
cards.eli5: It says HOW. In this way, likewise, secretly, well.

filled: the free man is a slave

cards.oneLine: Answers the question “in what way?”.
cards.mnemonic: When · How much · How · Where — How: manner.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The spirit level 🎚️ — how it was done. Most -ως adverbs are manner: ὁμοίως “likewise”, καλῶς “well”, δικαίως “justly”.
cards.spotIt: Ask “in what way?”. If the adverb is the answer, it is manner. An -ως ending is a strong hint.
cards.bookDef: Manner (In what way?)

examples.greek: *ὁμοίως* ὁ ἐλεύθερος κληθεὶς δοῦλός ἐστιν Χριστοῦ
examples.english: *Likewise* he who is called as a free man is Christ’s slave
examples.note: ὁμοίως says in what way: in the same way as the slave who is the Lord’s freedman in 7:22a.

cards.name: Adverb of Place
cards.eli5: It says WHERE. Here, there, outside.
cards.oneLine: Answers the question “where?”.
cards.mnemonic: When · How much · How · Where — Where: place.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The map pin 📌. ὧδε “here”, ἐκεῖ “there”, ἔξω “outside”, ἄνω “above”, κάτω “below”.
cards.spotIt: Ask “where?”. If the adverb is the answer, it is place.
cards.bookDef: Place (Where?)

examples.english: Sit *here* in a good place
examples.note: ὧδε says where: here. καλῶς beside it is manner — sit well, comfortably.

cards.name: Adverb Used as a Noun
cards.eli5: Put “the” in front of an “outside” word and it becomes a thing: THE OUTSIDE.
cards.oneLine: An adverb with the article, acting as a noun.
cards.mnemonic: Noun · Adjective — Noun: an adverb used as a noun.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The article is a noun-maker, just as it was for adjectives in ch. 5 and prepositional phrases here. τό + ἐκτός “outside” = “the outside”.
cards.spotIt: An article with no noun, and after it a single adverb. Supply “the” and make it a thing.
cards.bookDef: Adverbs used as nouns.
cards.watchOut: An article + a prepositional phrase does the same thing (τὰ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ). One word after the article: adverb. A preposition and its object: prepositional phrase.

examples.greek: ἵνα γένηται καὶ *τὸ ἐκτὸς* αὐτοῦ καθαρόν
examples.english: so *the outside* of it may also become clean
examples.note: τὸ ἐκτός is the subject of γένηται. An adverb, turned into a thing by the article.

cards.name: Adverb Used as an Adjective
cards.eli5: Tuck a “now” word between “the” and a noun and it describes the noun: the PRESENT time.
cards.oneLine: An adverb in attributive position, describing a noun like an adjective.
cards.mnemonic: Noun · Adjective — Adjective: an adverb used as an adjective.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The slot between an article and its noun belongs to adjectives (ch. 5, attributive position). Put an adverb in it and it becomes one: τῷ νῦν καιρῷ, “the now time”, the present time.
cards.spotIt: Is the adverb sandwiched between an article and its noun? Then it is describing that noun.
cards.bookDef: Adverbs used as adjectives.
cards.watchOut: Not the same as an adverb modifying an adjective (χαλεποὶ λίαν). There the adjective is already there and the adverb turns it up; here there is no adjective, and the adverb is doing its job.

examples.greek: πρὸς τὴν ἔνδειξιν τῆς δικαιοσύνης αὐτοῦ ἐν τῷ *νῦν* καιρῷ
examples.english: to demonstrate his righteousness at the *present* time (NIV)
examples.note: νῦν between τῷ and καιρῷ is in attributive position: which time? the present one. (The chart prints the reference as Rom 3:25; the phrase is in 3:26.)

cards.name: Particle of Intensification
cards.eli5: A word that says “yes, really!” and makes the sentence stronger.
cards.oneLine: A particle that intensifies the statement.
cards.mnemonic: Yes · Look — Yes: intensification.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Turn the volume up 🙌. ναί is “yes”; ἀμήν is the Hebrew “truly, so be it”; γέ is “even, indeed”.
cards.spotIt: Can you take the word out and the sentence still says the same thing, only less forcefully? And is it ναί, ἀμήν or γέ?
cards.bookDef: Some Greek particles serve to express an intensification of the statement. This class of particles includes ἀμήν [“amen”], γέ [“even”], and ναί [“yes!”].

examples.greek: *ναὶ* ἐρωτῶ καὶ σέ, γνήσιε σύζυγε, συλλαμβάνου αὐταῖς
examples.english: *Yes*, I also ask you, true partner, to help these women
examples.note: ναί adds force to the request. (The chapter prints the reference as Phil 4:2; the words are in 4:3.)

examples.english: *Amen!* Come, Lord Jesus!
examples.note: ἀμήν says “so be it” to the promise just made — “Surely I am coming soon.”

cards.name: Particle of Attention
cards.eli5: A word that makes you look. “Look!” “Oh!” “Woe!”

filled: the judge stands at the door

cards.oneLine: A particle that draws the reader’s attention — an interjection.
cards.mnemonic: Yes · Look — Look: attention.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Turn your head 👀. ἰδού “look!” (the old “behold”), οὐαί “woe!”, ὦ “O!” — which is why a vocative so often follows it.
cards.spotIt: Is it ἰδού, οὐαί or ὦ, standing outside the grammar of the sentence and making you look?
cards.bookDef: Some Greek particles draw the reader’s attention and could also be classified as interjections, such as ἰδού (“look!”), οὐαί (“woe!”), and ὦ (“O!”).
cards.watchOut: ὦ is the vocative’s companion from ch. 2 — direct address with emotion. The vocative is the case; ὦ is the particle.

examples.english: *O* woman, great is your faith! (ESV)
examples.note: ὦ followed by the vocative γύναι. ὦ adds feeling to the address.

examples.greek: *ἰδοὺ* ὁ κριτὴς πρὸ τῶν θυρῶν ἕστηκεν
examples.english: *Look*, the judge stands at the door!
examples.note: ἰδού takes no part in the grammar; it grabs the reader by the collar.

confusions.question: Predicate nominative or apposition?
confusions.test: Is there a verb?
confusions.answer: Verb ⇒ predicate nominative, a claim. Comma only ⇒ apposition, a label.
confusions.example: “Ivan is the student” (claim) vs “Ivan, the student, came to class” (label).

confusions.question: Absolute or hanging?
confusions.test: Does a pronoun later in the sentence pick the word back up?
confusions.answer: No rope ⇒ absolute. Hangs by a pronoun ⇒ hanging.
confusions.example: Mark 1:1 “The beginning of the gospel…” (a headline) vs Matt. 13:38 “the good seed — THESE are the sons…” (a rope).

confusions.question: Address or subject?
confusions.test: Talked about, or talked to?
confusions.answer: About ⇒ subject. To ⇒ address, however much it looks like a subject.
confusions.example: “Husbands love their wives” (subject) vs “Husbands, love your wives” (address).

confusions.question: Two nominatives, one verb — which is the subject?
confusions.test: Run PAP: pronoun, then article, then proper name.
confusions.answer: First yes wins. In John 1:1c ὁ λόγος has the article, so it is the subject and θεός is the predicate — definite, not “a god”.
confusions.example: καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος.

confusions.question: Cognate or plain direct object?
confusions.test: Does the object echo the verb — same root, or same idea?
confusions.answer: Echo ⇒ cognate. No echo ⇒ just the object. Either way it is still the object.
confusions.example: “Fight the good fight” (echo) vs “I hit Ivan” (no echo).

confusions.question: Two accusatives side by side — renamed, or called something?
confusions.test: Is there a verb doing the naming?
confusions.answer: A verb calls, makes or gives it something ⇒ complement. No verb between them, the second just says which one exactly ⇒ apposition.
confusions.example: “I have called you FRIENDS” · “they chose Stephen, a man full of faith”.

confusions.question: Accusative of respect or direct object?
confusions.test: Put “with respect to” in front of it.
confusions.answer: Better ⇒ respect. Worse ⇒ direct object.
confusions.example: “pierced WITH RESPECT TO the heart” — better. “I hit WITH RESPECT TO Ivan” — worse.

confusions.question: Subjective or objective?
confusions.test: Turn the head noun into a verb. Is X doing it, or getting it?
confusions.answer: Doing it ⇒ subjective. Getting it ⇒ objective.
confusions.example: “the love of Christ” — Christ loving (subjective) or Christ being loved (objective). The Greek is identical either way.

confusions.question: Source or separation? Both say “from”.
confusions.test: Is the “from” attached to a noun or to a verb?
confusions.answer: Where a noun came from ⇒ source. What a verb moves away from ⇒ separation.
confusions.example: “the righteousness from God” (source) vs “depart from the faith” (separation).

confusions.question: Genitive direct object or objective genitive?
confusions.test: What is the genitive hanging off — a verb or a noun?
confusions.answer: Off a verb ⇒ genitive direct object. Off a noun ⇒ objective genitive.
confusions.example: “you did not lack anything” (verb) vs “faith in God” (noun).

confusions.question: Partitive or material/content?
confusions.test: Is the genitive the whole the head noun is a slice of, or the stuff the head noun is made of?
confusions.answer: Whole ⇒ partitive. Stuff ⇒ material or content.
confusions.example: “one of the boats” (a slice of the fleet) vs “a cup of water” (what fills the cup).

confusions.question: Possession or relationship?
confusions.test: Is the genitive owning a thing, or being kin to a person?
confusions.answer: Owns a thing ⇒ possession. Family, with “son of” or “wife of” left out ⇒ relationship.
confusions.example: “the house of Philip” (owns it) vs “James the [son] of Zebedee” (kin).

confusions.question: Attributive or description?
confusions.test: Can the genitive be rewritten as an adjective?
confusions.answer: Becomes a real adjective ⇒ attributive. Nothing more specific fits ⇒ description, the catch-all.
confusions.example: “the word of his power” → “his powerful word” (attributive) vs “a baptism of repentance” (description).

confusions.question: Vocative, or nominative of address?
confusions.test: What shape is the word in?
confusions.answer: Vocative shape ⇒ vocative of direct address. Nominative shape doing the same job ⇒ nominative of address.
confusions.example: Λάζαρε (vocative) vs οἱ ἄνδρες, “Husbands…” (nominative doing a vocative’s work).

confusions.question: Means or agency?
confusions.test: Could the dative have refused?
confusions.answer: A thing with no will ⇒ means. A person who chose ⇒ agency.
confusions.example: “cutting himself with stones” (means) vs “led by the Spirit” (agency).

confusions.question: Three uses all come out “with”. Which one?
confusions.test: Tool, style, or company?
confusions.answer: A tool ⇒ means. A style ⇒ manner. Company ⇒ association, often with a συν- verb.
confusions.example: “with stones” · “openly” · “buried with him”.

confusions.question: Place or sphere?
confusions.test: Could you point at it?
confusions.answer: A real spot ⇒ place. A realm you can only imagine ⇒ sphere.
confusions.example: “sitting in a circle” (place) vs “sighing in his spirit” (sphere).

confusions.question: Indirect object or personal interest?
confusions.test: Does the sentence hand something over, or say who gains and loses by it?
confusions.answer: Something is handed over and nothing is said about gain ⇒ indirect object. Somebody plainly benefits or suffers ⇒ personal interest. But the chapter says outright that every dative of advantage is also an indirect object, and that the label has to be inferred from context — so this one is a judgement call and worth saying so in class rather than answering flatly.
confusions.example: “give glory to God” (handed over) · “adorned for her husband” (benefits) · “don't store up for yourselves” (benefits).

confusions.question: Attributive or predicate?
confusions.test: Where is the article? Does it precede the adjective, or only the noun?
confusions.answer: The article precedes the adjective ⇒ attributive: ὁ ἀγαθὸς ἄνθρωπος, ὁ ἄνθρωπος ὁ ἀγαθός. The article precedes the noun and not the adjective ⇒ predicate: ἀγαθὸς ὁ ἄνθρωπος. No article on either word ⇒ it could be either, and context decides: ἄνθρωπος ἀγαθός.
confusions.example: ὁ ἀγαθὸς ἄνθρωπος “the good man” · ἀγαθὸς ὁ ἄνθρωπος “the man is good” · ἄνθρωπος ἀγαθός — either.

confusions.question: Comparative or elative?
confusions.test: Is there anything on the other side of the scale?
confusions.answer: Something to compare against ⇒ comparative. Nothing ⇒ elative, and translate it “very”.
confusions.example: “more powerful than I” (comparative) vs “a very large crowd” (elative).

confusions.question: No article — indefinite, or Colwell?
confusions.test: Is it a predicate nominative sitting in front of the to-be verb?
confusions.answer: In front of the copula ⇒ Colwell explains the missing article, and the noun can still be definite. Elsewhere, run the three questions: a? quality? or still THE?
confusions.example: θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος — Colwell, definite. πλοιάριον in Mark 3:9 — genuinely “a”.

confusions.question: Two accusative objects — which double is it?
confusions.test: Slip “as” between them.
confusions.answer: “As” fits ⇒ object + complement. “As” is nonsense and one of them is a person ⇒ person + thing.
confusions.example: “gave his life AS a ransom” · “asks him for bread”.

confusions.question: Articular or anarthrous?
confusions.test: Is there a ὁ, ἡ or τό in front of it?
confusions.answer: There is ⇒ articular, the joint is in place. There is not ⇒ anarthrous, ἀν- plus ἄρθρον. The word only names what is there; what an absence means is the separate three-way question under Poof.
confusions.example: John 1:1 has both in one clause: ὁ λόγος articular, θεός anarthrous.

confusions.question: A time expression — which case?
confusions.test: Ask what the phrase is measuring.
confusions.answer: The point when it happened ⇒ dative. What kind of time, or time during which ⇒ genitive. How long it went on ⇒ accusative.
confusions.example: Luke 23:56b–24:1a has all three: τὸ σάββατον (accusative, how long they rested) · τῇ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων (dative, the day they came) · ὄρθρου βαθέως (genitive, what kind of hour).

confusions.question: τίς or τις — asking, or anyone?
confusions.test: Look for its own accent, where it stands, and a question mark.
confusions.answer: τίς/τί with its own acute, often first, and a ; at the end ⇒ interrogative, “who? what?”. τις/τι leaning on the word before, never first, no question ⇒ indefinite, “someone, anyone”.
confusions.example: τί κωλύει με βαπτισθῆναι; (Acts 8:36) · ἐάν τις εἴπῃ (1 John 4:20).

confusions.question: Yourselves, or one another?
confusions.test: Does the action stay with each person, or cross over to the others?
confusions.answer: Each one to himself ⇒ reflexive, ἑαυτούς. Each one to the others ⇒ reciprocal, ἀλλήλων.
confusions.example: ἑαυτοὺς πειράζετε (2 Cor 13:5) · ἀνεχόμενοι ἀλλήλων (Col 3:13).

confusions.question: Does the prepositional phrase hang on a verb or a noun?
confusions.test: Where is the article? Then ask “how?” or “which?”.
confusions.answer: Tucked between an article and its noun, or introduced by its own article after the noun ⇒ adjectival, “which one?”. Otherwise it usually hangs on the verb ⇒ adverbial, “how, where, when, why?”.
confusions.example: αἰτείτω ἐν πίστει (Jas 1:6) · τῇ κατ᾽ εὐσέβειαν διδασκαλίᾳ (1 Tim 6:3).

confusions.question: An article with no noun — what is standing in for the noun?
confusions.test: Count what comes after the article.
confusions.answer: A preposition and its object ⇒ substantival prepositional phrase. A single adverb ⇒ adverb used as a noun. Either way, supply “the thing(s)”.
confusions.example: τὰ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ (1 John 2:15) · τὸ ἐκτός (Matt 23:26).

confusions.question: Adverb modifying an adjective, or used as one?
confusions.test: Is there an adjective already there?
confusions.answer: Yes, and the adverb turns it up ⇒ modifying an adjective (χαλεποὶ λίαν). No, and the adverb sits between article and noun ⇒ used as an adjective (τῷ νῦν καιρῷ).
confusions.example: Matt 8:28 · Rom 3:26.

confusions.question: In order that, or so that?
confusions.test: Was it the aim, or the outcome?
confusions.answer: What someone meant to happen ⇒ purpose, typically ἵνα. What actually came of it ⇒ result, typically ὥστε. ὅπως can be either, so the word alone does not settle it.
confusions.example: John 3:16 has both: ὥστε … ἔδωκεν (result), ἵνα … μὴ ἀπόληται (purpose).

confusions.question: ὅτι — “because” or “that”?
confusions.test: Look at the verb before it.
confusions.answer: A verb of saying, thinking, knowing, seeing or hearing ⇒ declarative, it gives the content (“that”, or quotation marks). Otherwise, if it gives a reason ⇒ causal, “because”.
confusions.example: ὅτι αὐτῶν ἐστιν ἡ βασιλεία (Matt 5:3) · εἴπῃ ὅτι Ἀγαπῶ (1 John 4:20).

confusions.question: δέ — “and” or “but”?
confusions.test: Does the new clause push against the last one?
confusions.answer: It simply adds or moves on ⇒ copulative, “and” (or nothing at all). It sets up a contrast ⇒ adversative, “but”.
confusions.example: ἡμεῖς δὲ οὐκ ἐσμὲν ὑποστολῆς (Heb 10:39): “But we” — set against those who shrink back.

confusions.question: οὖν or γάρ — which way does the arrow point?
confusions.test: Is the clause a conclusion, or a reason?
confusions.answer: A conclusion drawn from what went before ⇒ inferential, οὖν “therefore”. A reason for what went before ⇒ explanatory, γάρ “for”.
confusions.example: Παρακαλῶ οὖν ὑμᾶς (Rom 12:1) · Οὕτως γὰρ ἠγάπησεν (John 3:16).

confusions.question: If, or even if?
confusions.test: Is there a καί glued to the εἰ or ἐάν?
confusions.answer: εἰ or ἐάν alone ⇒ conditional. εἰ καί, καὶ εἰ, κἄν, or καίπερ ⇒ concessive: granted, and it still does not stop the main clause.
confusions.example: ἐὰν ὁμολογῶμεν (1 John 1:9) · καίπερ ὢν υἱός (Heb 5:8).

confusions.question: How much, or how?
confusions.test: Swap in “very” and then “in this way”.
confusions.answer: “To what extent?” ⇒ degree (λίαν, περισσόν, μᾶλλον). “In what way?” ⇒ manner (ὁμοίως, καλῶς, most -ως words).
confusions.example: περισσὸν ἔχωσιν (John 10:10) · ὁμοίως ὁ ἐλεύθερος (1 Cor 7:22).

extraQuiz.prompt: "Grace, mercy, peace from God our Father" (1 Tim. 1:2) — all nominative, no verb, opening a letter.
extraQuiz.why: Opening material, tied to nothing. A headline, not a rope.

extraQuiz.prompt: "You call me Teacher and Lord" (John 13:13) — the titles are nominative where you expected accusative.
extraQuiz.why: A title being used as the name people call him. Badges don't decline.

extraQuiz.prompt: "Son of David, have mercy on us" (Matt. 9:27).
extraQuiz.why: He is being called out to, not described.

extraQuiz.prompt: "Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus" (Rom. 1:1) — two nominatives, no verb.
extraQuiz.why: δοῦλος renames Παῦλος. No verb, so no claim — just a label.

extraQuiz.prompt: "He is our peace" (Eph. 2:14).
extraQuiz.why: A verb with a nominative each side. αὐτός is a pronoun, so it is the subject; ἡ εἰρήνη is what is said about him.

extraQuiz.prompt: "The good seed — these are the sons of the kingdom" (Matt. 13:38).
extraQuiz.why: σπέρμα is left dangling, but οὗτοι picks it up. Hanging by a pronoun.

extraQuiz.prompt: "Fight the good fight" (1 Tim. 1:18).
extraQuiz.why: The object echoes the verb — the same root, even.

extraQuiz.prompt: "He gave his life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45).
extraQuiz.why: Two accusatives, and “as” slips between them: object + complement. Slip "as" between the two accusatives — "his life AS a ransom" — so it is the complement, not the person-and-thing double.

extraQuiz.prompt: "They were cut to the heart" (Acts 2:37) — an inner wound, not a surgical one.
extraQuiz.why: Put “with respect to” in front and the sense improves.

extraQuiz.prompt: "Going a little farther, he fell on the ground" (Mark 14:35).
extraQuiz.why: μικρόν answers “how far?” — MMR, one of three.

extraQuiz.prompt: "Being justified freely by his grace" (Rom. 3:24).
extraQuiz.why: δωρεάν answers “how?” — MMR, two of three.

extraQuiz.prompt: "They chose Stephen, a man full of faith" (Acts 6:5).
extraQuiz.why: ἄνδρα renames the object. Alias.

extraQuiz.prompt: An infinitive's subject — the one performing the infinitive's action.
extraQuiz.why: Finite verbs take a nominative subject. Infinitives take an accusative one.

extraQuiz.prompt: "and the Word was God" (John 1:1c) — which use is θεός?
extraQuiz.why: ὁ λόγος has the article and wins the pecking order, so θεός is the predicate. No article, and still definite.

extraQuiz.english: Remember Lot's wife

extraQuiz.greek: καὶ Σίμων ὁ ζηλωτὴς καὶ Ἰούδας *Ἰακώβου* (Acts 1:13)
extraQuiz.english: and Simon the Zealot, and Judas son of James

extraQuiz.why: He is being called by name. The vocative has exactly one use, and this is it.

extraQuiz.prompt: δὸς δόξαν τῷ θεῷ (John 9:24) — the underlined τῷ θεῷ.
extraQuiz.why: Glory is handed over, and God is who it goes to. PORT — T.

extraQuiz.prompt: θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος (John 1:1) — why does θεός have no article?
extraQuiz.why: A definite predicate nominative in front of the copula usually drops it. Colwell drops.

extraQuiz.prompt: τοῦ μεγάλου θεοῦ καὶ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (Titus 2:13) — one article over both nouns.
extraQuiz.why: Singular, personal, non-proper, same case, joined by καί. Sharp joins them into one person.

extraQuiz.prompt: σὺ εἶ ὁ ἅγιος (John 6:69) — the underlined ὁ ἅγιος.
extraQuiz.why: An adjective with the article and no noun to describe. It has become the noun. ASAP — S.

extraQuiz.english: she came and knelt before him

ὁ γὰρ ἐσθίων καὶ πίνων κρίμα *ἑαυτῷ* ἐσθίει (1 Cor 11:29)
he eats and drinks judgment on himself

extraQuiz.english: he eats and drinks judgment on himself

ἐγὼ … *ὕδατι* βαπτίζω ὑμᾶς (Luke 3:16)
I baptise you with water
extraQuiz.greek: ἐγὼ … *ὕδατι* βαπτίζω ὑμᾶς (Luke 3:16)
extraQuiz.english: I baptise you with water
extraQuiz.why: Water is a tool with no will of its own. MAMA — M, not agency.

τί ποιεῖτε ὃ οὐκ ἔξεστιν *τοῖς σάββασιν*; (Luke 6:2)
Why are you doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath?
extraQuiz.greek: τί ποιεῖτε ὃ οὐκ ἔξεστιν *τοῖς σάββασιν*; (Luke 6:2)
extraQuiz.english: Why are you doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath?
extraQuiz.why: A point on the calendar. HIT — T.

extraQuiz.prompt:
ἀλλὰ *παρρησίᾳ* περὶ τοῦ πατρὸς ἀπαγγελῶ ὑμῖν (John 16:25)
but I will tell you plainly about the Father
extraQuiz.greek: ἀλλὰ *παρρησίᾳ* περὶ τοῦ πατρὸς ἀπαγγελῶ ὑμῖν (John 16:25)
extraQuiz.english: but I will tell you plainly about the Father
extraQuiz.why: The same word the chart files under manner at Mark 8:32. A style, not a tool. MAMA — M.

extraQuiz.prompt:
ἠκολούθει δὲ *τῷ Ἰησοῦ* Σίμων Πέτρος (John 18:15)
Simon Peter was following Jesus
extraQuiz.greek: ἠκολούθει δὲ *τῷ Ἰησοῦ* Σίμων Πέτρος (John 18:15)
extraQuiz.english: Simon Peter was following Jesus
extraQuiz.why: ἀκολουθέω is a verb of following, and the chart lists following. BEAD — D.

extraQuiz.prompt:
ὁ δὲ μαθητὴς ἐκεῖνος … *συν*εισῆλθεν *τῷ Ἰησοῦ* (John 18:15)
that disciple went in with Jesus
extraQuiz.greek: ὁ δὲ μαθητὴς ἐκεῖνος … *συν*εισῆλθεν *τῷ Ἰησοῦ* (John 18:15)
extraQuiz.english: that disciple went in with Jesus
extraQuiz.why: συν- on the verb is the giveaway: he went in alongside Jesus, not using him. MAMA — A.

extraQuiz.prompt:
ὥσπερ γὰρ ὑμεῖς ποτε ἠπειθήσατε *τῷ θεῷ* (Rom 11:30)
just as you once disobeyed God
extraQuiz.greek: ὥσπερ γὰρ ὑμεῖς ποτε ἠπειθήσατε *τῷ θεῷ* (Rom 11:30)
extraQuiz.english: just as you once disobeyed God
extraQuiz.why: ἀπειθέω is a verb of obeying — disobeying is the same list. BEAD — D.

extraQuiz.prompt:
νῦν δὲ ἠλεήθητε *τῇ τούτων ἀπειθείᾳ* (Rom 11:30)
now you have received mercy because of their disobedience
extraQuiz.greek: νῦν δὲ ἠλεήθητε *τῇ τούτων ἀπειθείᾳ* (Rom 11:30)
extraQuiz.english: now you have received mercy because of their disobedience
extraQuiz.why: Slot in “because of” and it holds. BEAD — B.

extraQuiz.prompt:
καθὼς θέλετε ἵνα ποιῶσιν *ὑμῖν* οἱ ἄνθρωποι, ποιεῖτε *αὐτοῖς* ὁμοίως (Luke 6:31)
as you want people to do to you, do the same to them

extraQuiz.english: as you want people to do to you, do the same to them

extraQuiz.prompt:
*συν*εζωοποίησεν *τῷ Χριστῷ* (Eph 2:5)
he made us alive together with Christ
extraQuiz.greek: *συν*εζωοποίησεν *τῷ Χριστῷ* (Eph 2:5)
extraQuiz.english: he made us alive together with Christ
extraQuiz.why: συν- again. Alongside Christ, not by means of him. MAMA — A.

extraQuiz.prompt:
*χάριτί* ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι (Eph 2:5)
by grace you have been saved
extraQuiz.greek: *χάριτί* ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι (Eph 2:5)
extraQuiz.english: by grace you have been saved
extraQuiz.why: Grace is the instrument, not a person acting. MAMA — M.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? Only the accusative, “each, in turn, up”.
extraQuiz.why: ἀνά — “each, in turn, up”. 13 times in the GNT. Anabaptists baptised again — ἀνά is “up”, “again”, “each in turn”. Only thirteen times in the NT, so recognise it and move on.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? Only the genitive, “in place of, instead of”.
extraQuiz.why: ἀντί — “in place of, instead of”. 22 times in the GNT. An ANTI-christ is one who sets himself up in place of Christ. ἀντί is substitution: a ransom ἀντὶ πολλῶν, “in place of many”.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? Only the genitive, “from, of”.
extraQuiz.why: ἀπό — “from, of”. 646 times in the GNT. APOstasy is falling away from; an APOstle is sent from. ἀπό is away from the edge of something.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? Only the accusative, “into, in, at”.
extraQuiz.why: εἰς — “into, in, at”. 1768 times in the GNT. Into. The accusative is the case of direction, and εἰς is the most accusative word there is: motion into.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? Only the genitive, “from, out of”.
extraQuiz.why: ἐκ — “from, out of”. 914 times in the GNT. EXit — ἐκ (ἐξ before a vowel) is out of from the inside. ἀπό leaves from the edge; ἐκ comes out from within.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? Only the dative, “in, into, by”.
extraQuiz.why: ἐν — “in, into, by”. 2752 times in the GNT. IN. The commonest preposition in the NT, and it only ever takes the dative — the case of place, of being in something.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? Only the genitive, “before, at”.
extraQuiz.why: πρό — “before, at”. 47 times in the GNT. PROlogue, the word before; PROphet, one who speaks before. πρό is before, in time or place.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? Only the dative, “with”.
extraQuiz.why: σύν — “with”. 128 times in the GNT. SYNagogue, where people gather with; SYNoptic, seeing with. σύν is together with, and dative like the dative of association.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? + genitive “through”; + accusative “because of”.
extraQuiz.why: διά — διά takes 2 cases — + genitive “through”; + accusative “because of”. 667 times in the GNT. DIAmeter goes through the circle. With the genitive, through; with the accusative, because of — the reason you went through.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? + genitive “against”; + accusative “according to”.
extraQuiz.why: κατά — κατά takes 2 cases — + genitive “against”; + accusative “according to”. 473 times in the GNT. CATAstrophe comes down against you. With the genitive, against; with the accusative, according to — the gospel κατὰ Μαθθαῖον.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? + genitive “with”; + accusative “after”.
extraQuiz.why: μετά — μετά takes 2 cases — + genitive “with”; + accusative “after”. 469 times in the GNT. METAphysics was the book shelved after the Physics. With the genitive, with (in company); with the accusative, after.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? + genitive “concerning”; + accusative “around”.
extraQuiz.why: περί — περί takes 2 cases — + genitive “concerning”; + accusative “around”. 333 times in the GNT. PERImeter goes around. With the accusative, around; with the genitive, concerning — talk that goes round a subject.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? + genitive “for”; + accusative “above”.
extraQuiz.why: ὑπέρ — ὑπέρ takes 2 cases — + genitive “for”; + accusative “above”. 150 times in the GNT. HYPER is over and above. With the accusative, above; with the genitive, for — on behalf of, standing over someone to shield them.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? + genitive “by”; + accusative “under”.
extraQuiz.why: ὑπό — ὑπό takes 2 cases — + genitive “by”; + accusative “under”. 220 times in the GNT. HYPOdermic goes under the skin. With the accusative, under; with the genitive, by — the agent behind a passive verb.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? + genitive “on, upon”; + dative “upon”; + accusative “against”.
extraQuiz.why: ἐπί — ἐπί takes 3 cases — + genitive “on, upon”; + dative “upon”; + accusative “against”. 890 times in the GNT. EPIdermis is the skin on top. ἐπί is on, upon — and with the accusative, against: coming down upon somebody.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? + genitive “from”; + dative “with”; + accusative “beside”.
extraQuiz.why: παρά — παρά takes 3 cases — + genitive “from”; + dative “with”; + accusative “beside”. 194 times in the GNT. PARAllel lines run beside each other; a PARAlegal works beside. With genitive from (beside someone), dative with, accusative beside.

extraQuiz.prompt: Which preposition? + genitive “for”; + dative “at”; + accusative “to”.
extraQuiz.why: πρός — πρός takes 3 cases — + genitive “for”; + dative “at”; + accusative “to”. 700 times in the GNT. PROSelyte, one who has come to. With the accusative, to or toward — ὁ λόγος ἦν πρὸς τὸν θεόν — which is nearly all its uses.

extraQuiz.prompt: By that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all
extraQuiz.greek: ἐν ᾧ θελήματι ἡγιασμένοι ἐσμὲν *διὰ τῆς προσφορᾶς* τοῦ σώματος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐφάπαξ (Heb 10:10)
extraQuiz.english: we have been sanctified *through the offering* of the body of Jesus Christ once for all
extraQuiz.why: διά is a preposition taking the genitive, so “through”. The phrase διὰ τῆς προσφορᾶς hangs on the verb ἡγιασμένοι ἐσμέν: it says how we were sanctified — adverbial. (Asked about the word alone: διά + genitive, means or agency.)

extraQuiz.prompt: sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all
extraQuiz.greek: ἐν ᾧ θελήματι ἡγιασμένοι ἐσμὲν διὰ τῆς προσφορᾶς τοῦ σώματος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ *ἐφάπαξ* (Heb 10:10)
extraQuiz.english: sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ *once for all*
extraQuiz.why: ἐφάπαξ is an adverb (ἐπί + ἅπαξ, “once”), and it answers “when?” or “how often?” — once, for all time. That is time. It could be argued as manner (“in a once-for-all way”); time is the more natural reading, but worth checking in class.

extraQuiz.prompt: Hurry and get out of Jerusalem quickly
extraQuiz.greek: σπεῦσον καὶ ἔξελθε ἐν τάχει *ἐξ Ἰερουσαλήμ*, διότι οὐ παραδέξονταί σου μαρτυρίαν περὶ ἐμοῦ (Acts 22:18)
extraQuiz.english: Hurry and get *out of Jerusalem* quickly
extraQuiz.why: ἐξ is ἐκ before a vowel — a preposition taking the genitive, “out of”. ἐξ Ἰερουσαλήμ hangs on the imperative ἔξελθε and says where from: adverbial.

extraQuiz.prompt: because they will not accept your testimony about me
extraQuiz.greek: σπεῦσον καὶ ἔξελθε ἐν τάχει ἐξ Ἰερουσαλήμ, *διότι* οὐ παραδέξονταί σου μαρτυρίαν περὶ ἐμοῦ (Acts 22:18)
extraQuiz.english: *because* they will not accept your testimony about me
extraQuiz.why: διότι is a subordinating conjunction on the chart’s causal row: it gives the reason Paul must leave.

extraQuiz.prompt: they will not accept your testimony about me
extraQuiz.greek: διότι οὐ παραδέξονταί *σου* μαρτυρίαν περὶ ἐμοῦ (Acts 22:18)
extraQuiz.english: they will not accept *your* testimony about me
extraQuiz.why: σου is the genitive singular of σύ — a personal pronoun, “your”, here possessive on μαρτυρίαν.

extraQuiz.prompt: But we ought always to give thanks to God for you
extraQuiz.greek: *ἡμεῖς* δὲ ὀφείλομεν εὐχαριστεῖν τῷ θεῷ πάντοτε περὶ ὑμῶν (2 Thess 2:13)
extraQuiz.english: But *we* ought always to give thanks to God for you
extraQuiz.why: ἡμεῖς is the personal pronoun “we”. ὀφείλομεν already says “we”, so the pronoun is emphatic: we, in contrast to those in 2:10–12.

extraQuiz.prompt: But we ought always to give thanks to God for you
extraQuiz.greek: ἡμεῖς *δὲ* ὀφείλομεν εὐχαριστεῖν τῷ θεῷ πάντοτε περὶ ὑμῶν (2 Thess 2:13)
extraQuiz.english: *But* we ought always to give thanks to God for you
extraQuiz.why: δέ is a coordinating conjunction, and it is on the chart twice. Here it sets “we” against those who perish and believe the lie in 2:10–12, so adversative, “but”. A reader who takes it as a simple transition would call it copulative — worth hearing in class.

extraQuiz.prompt: give thanks to God for you
extraQuiz.greek: ἡμεῖς δὲ ὀφείλομεν εὐχαριστεῖν τῷ θεῷ πάντοτε περὶ *ὑμῶν* (2 Thess 2:13)
extraQuiz.english: give thanks to God for *you*
extraQuiz.why: ὑμῶν is the genitive plural of σύ — personal pronoun, “you (all)”, the object of περί (“concerning, for”). ὑ has the u of YOU.
